takeaway: HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer had a 3-year overall survival of 82.4%, against 57.1% if HPV-negative. After adjustment the hazard ratio for death was 0.42 [1].
clinicalQuestion: Does tumour HPV status independently predict survival in oropharyngeal cancer?
background: Many oropharyngeal squamous cancers contain high-risk HPV, predominantly HPV-16, whose E6 and E7 proteins inactivate p53 and retinoblastoma protein [1].
studyDesign: Retrospective HPV analysis of a randomised radiotherapy trial (RTOG 0129).
setting: Patients treated with cisplatin plus either accelerated-fractionation or standard-fractionation radiotherapy.
population: 323 patients with oropharyngeal cancer who had HPV results; 206 (63.8%) were HPV-positive.
intervention: Accelerated-fractionation radiotherapy plus cisplatin, compared with standard fractionation plus cisplatin, with HPV analysed in the oropharyngeal subset.
comparator: HPV-negative tumours, and the alternate radiotherapy schedule.
primaryOutcome: Overall survival by tumour HPV status.
mainFindings: Median follow-up was 4.8 years. Accelerated and standard fractionation had similar 3-year overall survival (70.3% vs 64.3%; P = 0.18; hazard ratio for death 0.90; 95% CI 0.72 to 1.13). Among oropharyngeal cancers, HPV-positive tumours had 3-year overall survival of 82.4% (95% CI 77.2 to 87.6) versus 57.1% (48.1 to 66.1), and 3-year progression-free survival of 73.7% versus 43.4%. After adjustment for age, race, tumour and nodal stage, tobacco exposure, and treatment assignment, HPV positivity conferred a 58% reduction in the risk of death (hazard ratio 0.42; 95% CI 0.27 to 0.66). The risk of death rose with each additional pack-year of smoking. The authors conclude that tumour HPV status is a strong independent prognostic factor and that future trials should separate or stratify by HPV [1].
clinicalMeaning: Record HPV status and smoking history. Do not treat the two diseases as if they had the same prognosis [1].
limitations: This is a prognostic analysis inside a treatment trial, not a trial of de-escalation. It does not show that radiotherapy dose can be reduced [1].
bottomLine: HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer: 3-year survival 82.4% versus 57.1%, adjusted hazard ratio for death 0.42 [1].
practiceImplication: Test the tumour for HPV and quantify pack-years, because both mark survival in this study [1].
safetyOutcomes: Grade 3–4 acute toxicity was 80.0% with accelerated fractionation and 83.7% with standard fractionation (P = 0.21).
trustRationale: Large randomised cohort with prespecified multivariable adjustment.
whatNotToOverclaim: Do not use this paper to justify omitting cisplatin or lowering the radiation dose.
